traveler: Katherine Johnson (Creola Katherine Coleman Goble Johnson)
title: The Counting Child and the Burnout Point: West Virginia, Langley, and the Arithmetic of Return
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Caswell County, the mother is born
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. MacTutor's genealogical reconstruction of the family background is the only source for Joylette Roberta Lowe's 1887 birth in Caswell County; no birth record was independently located. The pin is a county centroid, not a landmark, and month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: Joylette Roberta Lowe is born in Caswell County, on the North Carolina side of the Virginia line, twenty-two years after emancipation. She will become a teacher. She will marry a man who never went past the sixth grade and who can look at a standing tree and say how many board feet of lumber are inside it. Between them the household will run on two literacies, hers of the classroom and his of the counted world. The county keeps no landmark of this birth and no record of it that anyone has found. What is known is that the family moves north and west, into West Virginia.
suggested_refs: Caswell County, North Carolina, county records for the Lowe family

stops.name: Danville, the marriage on the Dan River
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The date and place come from MacTutor's genealogical reconstruction alone; no marriage record was independently located. The coordinate falls within about a kilometre of Danville city center.
stops.campa: Joshua McKinley Coleman marries Joylette Roberta Lowe in a mill town on the Dan River. He farms, he cuts timber, he works seasons at the Greenbrier hotel; she teaches. Four children will come, and for the sake of those four the household will eventually split itself in half, wintering a hundred and twenty miles from the farm so that the children can sit in a schoolroom their own county declines to build. Nothing in the record says the couple discussed that arrangement in advance. They simply carried it out, year after year, until the last child was through.
suggested_refs: Danville, Virginia, marriage records for 1909

stops.name: White Sulphur Springs, the youngest of four
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Creola Katherine Coleman is born in a Greenbrier County resort town where her father works at times for the hotel. She is the last of the four. Greenbrier County provides no public secondary school for Black children, a fact that will eventually move the whole household a hundred and twenty miles every autumn and bring it back every summer. Before any of that she counts, without being taught to: the steps from the porch to the road, the steps up to the church door, the dishes she washes and the forks she dries.
stops.quote: I counted everything. I counted the steps to the road, the steps up to church, the number of dishes and silverware I washed … anything that could be counted, I did.
stops.quote_source: NASA, 'Katherine Johnson: The Girl Who Loved to Count' (no occasion given in the source)
suggested_refs: The Greenbrier hotel, White Sulphur Springs, where Joshua Coleman worked seasonally
sources: NASA, 'Katherine Johnson: The Girl Who Loved to Count' (nasa.gov)

stops.name: Institute, the high school on a college campus
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and the approximate year; the month of entry is not given in the sources, and 09-01 orders the stop to the academic year.
stops.campa: Joshua Coleman moves his wife and four children a hundred and twenty miles to Institute for the school year and drives back to the farm alone, and does it again the next year, and the next. The arrangement costs him two households and a great deal of driving, and no one in the family appears to have called it a sacrifice. Katherine, already advanced twice past her age, walks into the laboratory high school run on the campus of West Virginia State College at ten years old. She graduates from it at fourteen.
suggested_refs: The West Virginia State College laboratory high school, Institute, West Virginia

stops.name: Institute, the college that ran out of courses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the enrollment year; the month is not specified and 09-01 orders the stop. The Evans quotation below is [R]: MacTutor prints it as Johnson's own recollection without naming the underlying interview.
stops.campa: At fourteen she enters West Virginia State College and works through its mathematics offerings faster than the catalogue can hold her. Angie Turner King, a chemist, teaches her. James Carmichael Evans settles the question of her major without much ceremony. William Waldron Schieffelin Claytor, the third Black American to earn a doctorate in mathematics, tells her he is preparing her to be a research mathematician, and puts new courses on the schedule for a single student to take, analytic geometry of space among them.
stops.quote: I know how good you are in French, but you will also major in mathematics.
stops.quote_source: James Carmichael Evans to Katherine Coleman, as she recalled it; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Katherine Johnson'
suggested_refs: W. W. Schieffelin Claytor's teaching at West Virginia State College, 1930s

stops.name: Institute, summa cum laude at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and honors; the graduation month is not specified in the sources and 05-01 orders the stop.
stops.campa: She takes the degree summa cum laude at eighteen, in mathematics and French, from a college that widened its curriculum to keep pace with her. She is the youngest person on the platform by several years. Claytor has told her she would make a research mathematician. In 1937 there is no institution in the United States that will hire a Black woman as one, so the credential points at a profession that will not have her. She goes looking for work in the field that is open to her. She takes a job teaching school.
stops.quote: Many professors tell you that you'd be good at this or that, but they don't always help you with that career path. Professor Claytor made sure I was prepared to be a research mathematician.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson on W. W. Schieffelin Claytor; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Katherine Johnson'
suggested_refs: West Virginia State College commencement records, 1937

segments.name: The Schoolroom and the Test Case

stops.name: Marion, mathematics, French, and music
stops.date_confidence: the post is attested; its dates are contradicted inside the sources. MacTutor's narrative places her first teaching post from 1937, while its own career timeline gives 1939-1943 for Marion, which collides with the 1939 West Virginia University admission. Not resolved here. 09-01 orders the stop.
stops.campa: In a segregated Black public school in Smyth County she teaches mathematics, French, and music, three subjects because the school can pay for one teacher to cover them. She tells her students there is no such thing as a stupid question, only the one nobody asked, and she goes on saying it for the next eighty years. She is standing in front of a class when the Supreme Court alters her situation without intending to. How long she stays at this school is genuinely unclear: the sources put her here in two different and incompatible sets of years, and neither can be made to fit the other.
stops.quote: There's no such thing as a dumb question. It's dumb if you don't ask.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson, oral history interview, American Archive of Public Broadcasting, cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42
suggested_refs: Segregated Black public schooling in Smyth County, Virginia, in the late 1930s
sources: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, oral history cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42

stops.name: Morgantown, three students admitted under a court order
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and fact; the month is not specified and 09-01 orders the stop to the academic year. Her marriage to James Francis Goble is dated 1939 by MacTutor with no place given beyond West Virginia, so it gets no pin of its own and is carried here.
stops.campa: Gaines v. Canada obliges West Virginia to admit Black students to graduate programs it refuses to duplicate for them. John W. Davis, president of West Virginia State College, is asked to select three. He selects two men and Katherine Coleman Goble. She enrolls in mathematics at West Virginia University and becomes the first Black woman to do graduate work there, entering a department that the law had closed to her the previous spring. She has married James Francis Goble the same year.
stops.quote: I want to be a research mathematician.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson, oral history interview, American Archive of Public Broadcasting, cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42
suggested_refs: Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938) and its effect on West Virginia graduate admissions
sources: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, oral history cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42

stops.name: Morgantown, the term that ends in a pregnancy
stops.date_confidence: attested as to fact and year; the month of withdrawal is not recorded and 06-01 orders the stop.
stops.campa: She leaves after a term, pregnant, and does not go back. No degree, no thesis, no supervisor's name anywhere in the record of it. The next thirteen years go to three daughters and to teaching school, and the mathematics she was trained for waits that long for a federal agency to want it. The university that admitted her under compulsion loses track of her inside a year, and will have nothing further to say about her until she is ninety-seven. Nothing in the sources says she treated the withdrawal as final at the time.
suggested_refs: West Virginia University graduate mathematics enrollment records, 1939-1940

stops.name: Newport News, the move made for a job
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; no month is recorded, and 01-01 orders the stop ahead of the June hire.
stops.campa: The family moves to Newport News so that Katherine can report to the Langley laboratory across the water in Hampton and James Goble can look for work. It is a career migration undertaken as a couple, with three daughters and one salary that is not yet certain. She has not worked as a mathematician since the Morgantown term collapsed thirteen years earlier, and the agency about to hire her does not call the work mathematics. It calls the workers computers, and it sorts them by race before it sorts them by anything else. She is thirty-four years old.
suggested_refs: Black federal employment at NACA Langley in the early 1950s

stops.name: Langley Field, reporting to the West Area computers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month.
stops.campa: She reports in June to the West Area Computing unit, the pool of Black women mathematicians the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics keeps separated by building, by cafeteria table, and by bathroom, under the supervision of Dorothy Vaughan. Their job title is computer, which at Langley in 1953 is a thing a person is. They take the engineers' flight data and reduce it by hand and by desktop calculating machine. Her own account of the place, given decades later, is not the account the films give.
stops.quote: I didn't feel the segregation at NASA because everybody there was doing research.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson, oral history interview, American Archive of Public Broadcasting, cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42
suggested_refs: Dorothy Vaughan and the West Area Computing unit, NACA Langley, 1943-1958
sources: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, oral history cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42

stops.name: Langley Field, the loan that was never returned
stops.date_confidence: the two-week loan and the branch are attested; the exact date is not, and 07-01 orders the stop roughly two weeks after the June hire.
stops.campa: Two weeks after she arrives she is lent to the Maneuver Loads Branch of the Flight Research Division, and the engineers there never send her back. She works gust loads and wake turbulence for about four years, including the investigation of a crash attributed to the wake of a larger aircraft. She also asks questions. She asks the engineers what happened in the editorial briefings, which are closed to women, and then asks why she cannot go to them herself, and then keeps asking.
stops.quote: These were such intelligent men, they knew so much, and I always loved intelligence, and so I'd ask what had gone on in the briefings - I'd listen and listen and ask questions. Then, of course, I'd ask why I couldn't go myself, and eventually they just got tired of answering all my questions and just let me in to the briefings.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson on the Langley editorial briefings; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Katherine Johnson'
suggested_refs: Maneuver Loads Branch, Flight Research Division, NACA Langley

stops.name: Newport News, the death of James Goble
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; MacTutor gives the place only as Virginia, and the pin is set at the family home in Newport News. The day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: James Francis Goble dies of an inoperable brain tumor in December, three years into the Langley job. Katherine is thirty-eight, with three daughters. She keeps working because the salary is the household's only income and because she wants the work, and she is the sole support of the house from that December onward. She stays at the same desk in the Maneuver Loads Branch, on gust loads and wake turbulence, through the year that follows. Nothing in the sources says she took any leave.
suggested_refs: Obituary notices for James Francis Goble, Virginia, December 1956

stops.name: Langley Field, Sputnik and the six hundred pages
stops.date_confidence: the Sputnik launch date is attested. Johnson's contribution to the compendium is attested without a date of its own, and the stop is dated to the launch that occasioned the work.
stops.campa: A Soviet satellite passes over Virginia beeping on two frequencies, and within months the aeronautics laboratory has become a spaceflight laboratory. Langley's engineers assemble a compendium of roughly six hundred pages called Notes on Space Technology, a course of lectures in a subject with no textbook, because nobody has yet done the thing the subject is about. The small group reading those notes will become the Space Task Group, and Johnson is in it. She supplies mathematics for the compendium.
stops.quote: Everything was so new - the whole idea of going into space was new and daring. There were no textbooks, so we had to write them.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson on the years after Sputnik; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Katherine Johnson'
suggested_refs: Notes on Space Technology, NACA Langley internal compendium, 1958

stops.name: Langley Field, the letterhead changes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the establishment of NASA and the redesignation of the laboratory.
stops.campa: On the first of October the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics is dissolved into a new civilian agency, and Langley Memorial Aeronautical Laboratory becomes Langley Research Center. The reorganization abolishes the West Area Computing unit and distributes its women into the engineering groups they had been serving from a distance for fifteen years. Johnson had been distributed five years early, by a branch that borrowed her and quietly kept her. The segregated pool she was hired into no longer exists on paper.
stops.quote: We were pioneers of the space era. We worked in secret for about three years, often without knowing exactly what the total thrust of our work was.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson on the early space program; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Katherine Johnson'
suggested_refs: The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 and the dissolution of NACA

stops.name: Newport News, the choir at Carver Memorial
stops.date_confidence: the marriage year is attested. The meeting through church and family networks is attested without a date, and 01-01 orders the stop. The pin is the Newport News congregation's neighborhood near 36.99, -76.42; Nominatim returns no record for the church itself and the street address is unconfirmed. One research lens placed this point in Hampton, about nine kilometres away, which is corrected here.
stops.campa: She sings in the choir at Carver Memorial Presbyterian and belongs to that congregation for roughly fifty years. Through church and family she meets James A. Johnson, an Army officer home from Korea, and marries him. He takes on three daughters and a wife whose working days he is largely not cleared to hear about. His surname is the one that will stand on every NASA technical report she publishes, and he had it long before either of them knew there would be reports. The marriage runs sixty years.
suggested_refs: Carver Memorial Presbyterian Church, Marshall Avenue corridor, Newport News, Virginia

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the first report with a woman's name on it
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication of NASA TN D-233; the day is not specified and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: With the engineer Ted H. Skopinski she works out where a satellite's booster must burn out, and at what azimuth, so that the capsule comes down over a chosen point on a turning Earth. The problem is spherical geometry and it is also logistics, because a splashdown is a place where ships have to be waiting already. NASA Technical Note D-233 goes out in September with two names on the cover. It is the first research report out of the Flight Research Division that NASA credits to a woman, and she had to fight for the credit.
stops.quote: We needed to be assertive as women in those days - assertive and aggressive - and the degree to which we had to be that way depended on where you were. I had to be. In the early days of NASA women were not allowed to put their names on the reports - no woman in my division had had her name on a report.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson on authorship credit at NASA; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Katherine Johnson'
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-233, 'Determination of Azimuth Angle at Burnout for Placing a Satellite over a Selected Earth Position' (1960)
sources: NASA Technical Reports Server, catalog record for NASA TN D-233

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the trajectory for Freedom 7
stops.date_confidence: attested. The stop is dated to the flight; the calculations precede it by weeks. The pin is Langley, where the work was done, not Cape Canaveral, where the rocket stood; Johnson was not present at the launch.
stops.campa: Alan Shepard rides a Redstone up and back down in fifteen minutes, and the arc he travels is a parabola somebody computed in advance: when to launch, where he will come down, how the capsule meets the water. Johnson does that analysis. It is the first American flight with a man inside it and the simplest trajectory the program will ever fly, which is exactly why it can be checked by hand. The widely repeated claim that she alone sent Shepard into space compresses a mission design done by a whole division onto one desk.
suggested_refs: Mercury-Redstone 3 (Freedom 7) flight documentation, 5 May 1961

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the desk machine against the IBM
stops.date_confidence: the flight date is attested. NASA's own 2015 account states plainly that Glenn requested she personally recheck the electronic computer's figures before the flight. The vivid 'get the girl' phrasing circulates only in post-2016 retellings, and one investigation is reported to have found no contemporaneous 1962 document fixing the exact wording. The Glenn line below is [R]: NASA prints it as Johnson's memory of him speaking, not as a record of his speech.
stops.campa: Friendship 7 will be flown on numbers produced by an IBM 7090, and the IBM 7090 is new, and John Glenn is the one who will be sitting on top of the rocket. He asks that the woman who does the orbital mechanics run the same equations by hand before he goes. She sits at a desktop calculating machine and works the orbit through point by point, over days, and the two sets of figures agree to the digit. Glenn launches on the twentieth of February, orbits three times, and comes back down into the Atlantic.
stops.quote: If she says they're good, then I'm ready to go.
stops.quote_source: John Glenn, as Katherine Johnson remembered him saying; NASA, 'Katherine Johnson Biography'
suggested_refs: Mercury-Atlas 6 (Friendship 7) preflight documentation, February 1962
sources: NASA, 'Katherine Johnson: The Girl Who Loved to Count' (nasa.gov, published 24 November 2015)

stops.name: Langley Research Center, Echo I and its rocket casing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication of NASA TN D-1366; the day is not specified and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: With Gertrude C. Westrick she tracks what a balloon does in orbit. Echo I is a hundred feet of aluminized mylar inflated in vacuum so that radio signals can be bounced off it, and it is so light for its size that sunlight pushes it around. Five hundred days of its behavior, and of its spent rocket casing tumbling along nearby, go into Technical Note D-1366. There is no crew in this problem and no countdown. There is only the question of where an object in orbit will actually be next week.
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-1366, 'The Orbital Behavior of the Echo I Satellite and Its Rocket Casing During the First 500 Days' (1962)
sources: NASA Technical Reports Server, catalog record for NASA TN D-1366

stops.name: Langley Research Center, coming down through the upper air
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication of NASA TN D-2379; the day is not specified and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: With Jack A. White she derives approximate solutions for the flight-path angle of a vehicle reentering the upper atmosphere. Approximate is the working word: the exact equations will not solve in closed form, and a capsule falling toward the ocean needs an answer a person can compute fast enough for it to matter. Nine more technical reports will follow over the next sixteen years, and her name is on all of them. In 1953 she had been hired to reduce data other people produced.
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-2379, 'Approximate Solutions for Flight-Path Angle of a Reentry Vehicle in the Upper Atmosphere' (1964)
sources: NASA Technical Reports Server, catalog record for NASA TN D-2379

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the geometry of the solar system
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication of NASA TN D-2890; month and day are not given and default to 01-01.
stops.campa: With W. Thomas Blackshear she studies the geometric parameters of the solar system as aids to interplanetary navigation: where the planets stand relative to one another, and what a ship between them could sight on in order to know where it is. Nothing on the agency's schedule goes to another planet. She writes the study anyway, in a building pointed entirely at the Moon and at a deadline, and the paper goes out with a NASA number on it like any other. She is forty-six.
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-2890, 'A Study of Solar-System Geometric Parameters for Use as Interplanetary Navigation Aids' (1965)
sources: NASA Technical Reports Server, catalog record for NASA TN D-2890

stops.name: Langley Research Center, a fix from a single sighting
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1967 from the NTRS catalogue record for NASA TN D-4246 (authors W. T. Blackshear, H. A. Hamer, K. G. Johnson). One research lens dated this to October 1967; the catalogue record is December and the October date is an error. The associated Lunar Orbiter and Apollo group achievement awards are reported in the research pool without an individual citation and are carried here as [R].
stops.campa: With Blackshear and Harold A. Hamer she publishes a midcourse guidance procedure that requires one position fix, taken by a crew member through an optical instrument, and nothing more. The premise of the paper is failure. The radio link to Earth is gone, the ground computers are unreachable, and the men in the capsule have a sextant, a chart, and their own arithmetic. She is also named among the recipients of Lunar Orbiter and Apollo group achievement awards for work behind the mapping of landing sites.
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-4246, 'Midcourse-Guidance Procedure with Single Position Fix Obtained from Onboard Optical Measurements' (December 1967)
sources: NASA Technical Reports Server, catalog record for NASA TN D-4246

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the timing of the rendezvous
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the work and the mission; no date attaches to the calculations themselves, and 01-01 of the landing year orders the stop ahead of 20 July.
stops.campa: The Lunar Module has to lift off the Moon and arrive in the same orbit, at the same instant, as the Command and Service Module coming around from the far side. Miss, and there is no second attempt. Johnson computes the timing that puts the two craft in the same place at the same moment, eight years after John F. Kennedy set the deadline the whole building has been working inside. Asked late in life which piece of her work she valued most, she names this one, and not the Glenn verification the world remembers.
suggested_refs: Lunar orbit rendezvous procedures for Apollo 11, July 1969

stops.name: Pocono Mountains, a small television screen
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was at a meeting in the Pocono Mountains and watched the landing on a small television with a few others. The frequently repeated detail that this was an Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority gathering is not supported by the sources checked here and is dropped. The coordinate is regional; no hall or resort was identified.
stops.campa: She is not at Langley and she is not in Mission Control. She is at a meeting in the Pocono Mountains, and when the hour comes the people there crowd around a small television screen to watch a man climb down a ladder onto ground whose arrival time she calculated. The film made about her forty-seven years later will place her in Houston that night, at a console. She was in Pennsylvania, standing behind other people's shoulders, watching the same grey pictures as everybody else.
suggested_refs: Contemporary accounts of the Apollo 11 landing broadcast, 20 July 1969

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the charts that were already written
stops.date_confidence: attested that backup navigation material she contributed to formed part of the resources drawn on in the Apollo 13 return; no date attaches to her own work on it, and 04-01 orders the stop to the accident. The popular claim that she personally saved the mission is a later compression and is [R].
stops.campa: An oxygen tank ruptures two days out, and the crew moves into the Lunar Module with the main computer dark and most of the power gone. What they have is a body of procedures and charts for getting home on optical sightings and hand calculation, written years earlier by people who assumed nothing would work. Johnson's guidance papers are part of that inheritance. She did not save Apollo 13, and she said so, in one form or another, for the rest of her life.
stops.quote: I certainly never expected any glory. I was just doing the job I was hired to do. … I was always proud of my work, but for Pete's sake, I didn't do anything alone.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson, quoted by the Katherine Johnson Foundation, 'Biography' (ellipsis as printed in the source)
suggested_refs: Apollo 13 contingency return procedures, April 1970

stops.name: Langley Research Center, one measurement and no ground
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication of NASA TN D-5963; the day is not specified and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Technical Note D-5963, with Harold A. Hamer: an approach guidance method using a single onboard optical measurement. Six months after Apollo 13 the question of what a crew can accomplish with a window, an instrument, and no help from the ground has stopped being hypothetical. She keeps working it. Hamer's name stands beside hers on seven papers between 1967 and 1980, and the arithmetic in them is meant to be done by a man in a capsule, in the time he has, with what he can hold.
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-5963, 'An Approach Guidance Method Using a Single Onboard Optical Measurement' (1970)

stops.name: Langley Research Center, Moon to Earth by hand
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1971 for NASA TN D-6343 and September 1971 for NASA TN D-6461, both with Hamer; this stop carries both and is dated to the earlier. A fourth paper in the series, TN D-6752 on simplified interplanetary guidance, follows in May 1972 and is noted here rather than given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: Two more papers in a single year, both with Hamer: midcourse and approach guidance requirements for simplified onboard control of Moon-to-Earth trajectories, then fixed-angle translunar guidance procedures using onboard optical measurements. The Apollo program is being cancelled around her as she writes them. The methods are for a kind of flight the United States is about to stop making. She refines them anyway and publishes a fourth in the series the following spring.
suggested_refs: NASA TN D-6343 (July 1971), TN D-6461 (September 1971), and TN D-6752 (May 1972), all with H. A. Hamer

stops.name: Langley Research Center, errors in a decoupled system
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication of NASA TP-1184; the day is not specified and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Technical Paper 1184, with Hamer, on the effects of errors in decoupled control systems. The subject has moved. Nobody is going to the Moon, and what the agency is planning now is enormous lightweight structures assembled in orbit, antennas and trusses and arrays hundreds of feet long, far too flexible to steer as though they were rigid bodies. She will spend the last decade of her career on the mathematics of steering things that bend. Push one end of such a thing and the far end arrives late, and then keeps going.
suggested_refs: NASA TP-1184, 'Effects of Errors on Decoupled Control Systems' (1978)

stops.name: Langley Research Center, a long flexible beam
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication of NASA TP-1740; the day is not specified and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Technical Paper 1740, with Hamer: decoupled control of a long flexible beam in orbit. The work of these years also carries her into Landsat studies and Space Shuttle studies, and her name appears on all of it, which had not been true of any woman in her division when she arrived. She is sixty-two, and the Shuttle is flying. The title of the paper is the problem stated as plainly as it can be stated: a bar in free fall that shakes when you touch one end of it.
suggested_refs: NASA TP-1740, 'Decoupled Control of a Long Flexible Beam in Orbit' (1980)

stops.name: Langley Research Center, thirty-three years
stops.date_confidence: the retirement year is attested. The month is given as August in one research lens and is not confirmed elsewhere; it is carried as [R] and orders the stop.
stops.campa: She retires from Langley after thirty-three years, seven months after Challenger broke apart over Florida and the program she had spent her working life computing for stopped flying. She had come in when the laboratory studied airplanes and its Black women mathematicians ate at a separate table. She goes out of a research center with her name on the reports, having begun on the gust loads that shake an airplane wing and finished on the shaking of a beam in vacuum.
stops.quote: I loved going to work every single day.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson on her thirty-three years at Langley; NASA, 'Katherine Johnson Biography'
suggested_refs: NASA Langley personnel records for the 1986 retirement

stops.name: Farmingdale, an honorary Doctor of Laws
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor. The coordinate is the Farmingdale State College campus; one research lens gave a point about 3.5 kilometres southwest, corrected here.
stops.campa: Twelve years into retirement, a state college on Long Island gives her an honorary Doctor of Laws. She is seventy-nine. The year before, the National Technical Association had named her Mathematician of the Year. This is what recognition looks like before the film: professional bodies and regional campuses, honoring a woman whose work is known to the people who do the same work and to nobody else. The audience is a few thousand families on a lawn in June, waiting for their own names to be read.
suggested_refs: SUNY Farmingdale commencement records, 4 June 1998
sources: NASA, 'Katherine Johnson Biography' (nasa.gov), list of honorary degrees

stops.name: Norfolk, an honorary Doctor of Science
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year from NASA's list of her honorary degrees; month and day are not given and default to 01-01.
stops.campa: Old Dominion University, across the water from Hampton, awards her an honorary Doctor of Science. She is ninety-one. Margot Lee Shetterly, who grew up in Hampton knowing these women as neighbors and church members rather than as a story, has not yet begun the book that will make them one. Nothing about the ceremony is national news. She has been retired for twenty-four years, and has lived the whole of that time about twenty miles from the laboratory where she did the work the degree is for.

stops.name: The White House, the Presidential Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the East Room venue is confirmed by the Obama White House ceremony record. The coordinate is the canonical White House pin.
stops.campa: In the East Room, Barack Obama hangs the Presidential Medal of Freedom on a ninety-seven-year-old woman and reads out thirty-three years at NASA and a refusal to be limited by race or by sex. Almost nobody watching has heard her name before that morning. Margot Lee Shetterly's book and the film taken from it are a year away, and after them the buildings and statues and doctorates arrive faster than a woman of ninety-seven can travel to collect them.
stops.quote: If I've done anything in my life to deserve any of this, it is because I had great parents who taught me simple but powerful lessons that sustained me in the most challenging times.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson, quoted by the Katherine Johnson Foundation, 'Biography'

stops.name: Morgantown, the university's own doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year from NASA's list of honorary degrees; month and day are not given and default to 01-01, which also orders the stop ahead of the May building announcement.
stops.campa: West Virginia University confers a Presidential Honorary Doctorate of Humane Letters. She had entered its graduate mathematics program in 1939 as one of three Black students admitted because a court had left the state no alternative, the only woman among the three, and left within the year with nothing. Seventy-six years later the institution grants a degree to the ninety-seven-year-old who never finished the term. What that term produced, in the way of a transcript or a supervisor's name, is not in the record at all.

stops.name: Langley Research Center, a building takes her name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the naming announcement and dedication. In the same week she received the Silver Snoopy Award from astronaut Leland Melvin.
stops.campa: NASA announces that its new forty-thousand-square-foot computational research building at Langley, thirty million dollars of data center, will be the Katherine G. Johnson Computational Research Facility. She is there. Taraji P. Henson, who is at that moment playing her in a film not yet released, sends a recorded message saying they should name the whole agency after her. The machines going into the building will do in a second what she did in a week with a desk calculator.
stops.quote: I'm so happy to see you giving more recognition to women.
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson at the naming ceremony, 5 May 2016; NASA, 'Computational Facility Named After Langley Human Computer Katherine Johnson'

stops.name: Hollywood, the standing ovation at the Dolby
stops.date_confidence: attested. The venue and date of the 89th Academy Awards are confirmed; the on-stage appearance is documented in NASA's biography and in contemporaneous coverage of the broadcast.
stops.campa: Taraji P. Henson, Janelle Monae, and Octavia Spencer come out to present an award and bring a ninety-eight-year-old woman on stage with them. The theatre rises. Hidden Figures had premiered in New York the previous December and reached wide release in January, and most of the people standing had learned that she existed about eight weeks earlier. The work they are applauding was finished before any of them were told about it, and the earliest of it was sixty-four years old that night.

stops.name: Langley Research Center, the ribbon at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: The facility opens formally and she attends the ribbon-cutting at ninety-nine, at a laboratory she first entered in 1953 as a member of a computing pool segregated by building and by cafeteria table. The West Area computers had no sign with anybody's name on it. This name is cut above the door of a data center. Very few people with a NASA building named for them are alive on the day it opens. She stands in front of the door and holds the scissors herself.

stops.date_confidence: attested to August 2018 for the unveiling and the associated STEM scholarship; the day is not given and defaults to 01. The coordinate is the West Virginia State University campus at Institute; one research lens gave a point about 6.5 kilometres west, corrected here.
stops.campa: A bronze of her is set up beside the Cole Complex on the campus at Institute, with a scholarship in her name established alongside it, at the college that once put a course on the schedule for a single fourteen-year-old because she had used up everything else it offered. The bronze stands about a hundred and twenty miles from the county that would not build her a high school, and students walk past it on their way to the mathematics department. She turns a hundred years old that month.

stops.name: Manassas, Katherine G. Johnson Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year from NASA's list of honors; month and day are not given and default to 01-01. The coordinate is George Mason University's Science and Technology Campus at 10900 University Boulevard; one research lens gave a point about 6 kilometres east, corrected here.
stops.campa: George Mason University names a building on its science and technology campus in Manassas for her. She is a hundred years old. By this point the naming of things after Katherine Johnson has acquired a momentum of its own, and the things chosen tend to be places where computation happens: data centers, engineering halls, rooms full of the machines that made her original job title obsolete. None of these buildings existed while she was doing the work they commemorate. She did that work on paper.

stops.name: Fairmont, the facility that checks other people's arithmetic
stops.date_confidence: NASA announced the renaming on 23 February 2019 under federal legislation. Some sources date the change to 2018 with a commemoration in 2019, and the two are not reconciled here. The coordinate is the facility's own, 39 25 48 N 80 11 52 W; the research lenses supplied three different points for this one building, all of them wrong, and they are corrected here.
stops.campa: NASA's Independent Verification and Validation Facility, whose entire function is to check other people's flight software before anyone flies on it, is renamed for the woman who checked the IBM 7090 by hand in 1962. The building tests code against what the code is supposed to do and refuses to sign off until the two agree. Of everything that now carries her name, this is the one whose job description is hers. It stands in her home state, about ninety miles north of White Sulphur Springs, and the renaming came by act of Congress.

stops.name: Newport News, the twenty-fourth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. NASA states she died at home; several obituaries place the death at a retirement facility, and the sources do not resolve the difference. No medical cause of death was made public, and no burial site is named on any institutional page that covers the death in detail.
stops.campa: She dies on a Monday morning at a hundred and one. NASA says she died at home, the obituaries say a retirement facility, and nobody printed a reconciliation. No cause of death was made public. No cemetery is named, no interment recorded, no memorial service described on the foundation's own pages or on NASA's or anywhere in the aggregated public record. Her name is cut into two federal buildings and painted on a cargo spacecraft. Where she is buried is not known outside the family.
stops.quote: if you lose your curiosity, then you stop learning
stops.quote_source: Katherine Johnson, oral history interview, American Archive of Public Broadcasting, cpb-aacip-535-7940r9nd42

stops.campa: Correspondence, family photographs, awards, honorary degree citations, and born-digital records go to the West Virginia and Regional History Center, given by her two daughters. The bulk of the collection dates from the last decade of her life, which is to say from the years after the world found out. The archive sits on the campus she was admitted to under a court order in 1939 and walked away from, without a degree, the following year. Her own memoir, written with the same two daughters, appears from Amistad in May 2021.

stops.name: Washington, the Congressional Gold Medal
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the ceremony. The authorization is solid: Public Law 116-68, 8 November 2019, granting Congressional Gold Medals to Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan, Mary Jackson, Christine Darden, and collectively to the women computers of NACA and NASA. The 18 September 2024 presentation date and the Capitol venue rest on the research pool's citation and could not be re-verified this session; the U.S. Mint page returned HTTP 403.
stops.campa: Congress had authorized the medals in November 2019, three months before she died. The statute names her, Dorothy Vaughan, Mary Jackson, and Christine Darden. Four and a half years later, in September 2024, the ceremony takes place, and her family stands in her place to receive it. A separate medal is struck for the women of the computing pools as a body, unnamed, because at the time nobody was writing the names down. That medal carries no list, and nobody has since compiled one.
